Texas had a population of about **28,635,442**, according to the ACS 2020 5-year estimates (2016–2020).

- This is the sum of all 18,638 Texas census block groups.
- It's a survey estimate averaged over 2016–2020. It's not a count for a single point in time, and it's not the 2020 decennial Census count.
- I took "Texas" to mean the state. Texas County, Missouri and Texas County, Oklahoma also exist, so let me know if you meant one of those.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over block groups.

The 2020 ACS 5-year release (covering 2016–2020) puts the US population at about **326,569,308** for the 50 states and DC. Counting Puerto Rico as well, the total is **329,824,950**.

| Area | Population |
|---|---|
| 50 states + DC | 326,569,308 |
| Puerto Rico | 3,255,642 |

This is a survey estimate averaged over five years, not the 2020 Census count, so it won't match the decennial census exactly. The total adds up 242,335 block groups. Each block-group figure is an estimate with some sampling error.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over block groups. Puerto Rico was identified by GEOID prefix 72.

Using the 2020 ACS 5-year release (2016–2020), the five states with the highest share of residents aged 65 and over are **Maine (20.6%), Florida (20.5%), West Virginia (19.9%), Vermont (19.4%) and Delaware (18.8%)**.

| Rank | State | Total population | Aged 65+ | Share 65+ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Maine | 1,340,825 | 276,567 | 20.6% |
| 2 | Florida | 21,216,924 | 4,347,912 | 20.5% |
| 3 | West Virginia | 1,807,426 | 360,246 | 19.9% |
| 4 | Vermont | 624,340 | 120,872 | 19.4% |
| 5 | Delaware | 967,679 | 182,024 | 18.8% |

The next two states are Montana (18.7%) and Hawaii (18.4%). Puerto Rico isn't a state, but it would rank near the top at 20.5%, essentially tied with Florida. These are survey estimates with sampling error, so small differences between places, such as Maine vs. Florida, shouldn't be read as definitive.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01001 (Sex by Age). The 65+ count is the sum of fields B01001e20–e25 (men) and B01001e44–e49 (women), divided by B01001e1 (total population), with both summed over block groups.

About **$99,300** (2020 dollars), but this is an estimate. The dataset only has medians for each block group, and the exact county median can't be calculated from those. So I worked it out from the household income brackets for the whole county.

**How I estimated it (ACS 2020 5-year, 2016–2020):**
- King County has **900,061 households**. The middle one is household number 450,031 when sorted by income.
- 346,486 households earn under $75,000, and 453,017 earn under $100,000. So the middle household falls in the **$75,000–$99,999** bracket, near its top.
- Assuming incomes are spread evenly within that bracket puts the median at about **$99,300**.

**Related figures:**
| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Estimated median household income (from brackets) | ~$99,300 |
| Mean household income (total household income ÷ households) | $134,707 |
| Households earning $200,000 or more | 170,181 (18.9%) |

The mean is much higher than the median because a large share of households earn over $200,000, which pulls the average up. These figures are built from block-group survey data, which has sampling error.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B19001 (Household Income), fields B19001e1–B19001e17, and B19025 (Aggregate Household Income), field B19025e1, summed over block groups with GEOID prefix 53033 (King County, WA).

The ACS 2020 5-year estimates put Harris County, Texas at about **1,795,219 housing units**.

I can't give a population for the City of Austin from this dataset, because it only goes down to counties and census block groups and doesn't include city boundaries.

The closest figure I can give is for **Travis County, TX**, where most of Austin is: **1,250,884 people**, from the ACS 2020 5-year release (2016–2020).

This isn't the same as Austin's city population, for two reasons:
- Travis County also includes people who live outside Austin, in other towns and unincorporated areas.
- Parts of Austin are in Williamson and Hays counties, so those residents aren't in this number.

I can't measure change since 2010 with this dataset. It only has two ACS 5-year releases: 2019 (covering 2015–2019) and 2020 (covering 2016–2020). Nothing from 2010 is in it.

The closest comparison I can make is California's total population in those two releases:

| Release | Survey years | California population |
|---|---|---|
| ACS 2019 5-year | 2015–2019 | 39,283,497 |
| ACS 2020 5-year | 2016–2020 | 39,346,023 |
| **Difference** | | **+62,526 (+0.2%)** |

**This isn't a real year-over-year change.** The two releases share four of their five survey years (2016–2019), so the difference mostly reflects swapping 2015 out for 2020. It doesn't show how the population changed over that time. The Census Bureau advises comparing 5-year periods that don't overlap. Both numbers are also survey estimates with sampling error.

For a true 2010-to-now comparison, you'd need a source outside this dataset, such as the 2010 and 2020 Decennial Censuses or the Census Bureau's annual population estimates.

I can give you 2019, but not 2021. This dataset has only two releases, 2019 and 2020, so there's no 2021 figure. I've included the 2020 release instead, since it's the most recent one available. I took "Texas" to mean the state, not Texas County in Missouri or Oklahoma.

| Release | Survey years covered | Texas population |
|---|---|---|
| ACS 2019 5-year | 2015–2019 | 28,260,856 |
| ACS 2020 5-year | 2016–2020 | 28,635,442 |

**About these numbers:**
- Each figure is an average over five years of surveys. It isn't a count for one year.
- The two releases share four of their five survey years (2016–2019). The difference between them (about 374,600) is therefore not a real year-over-year change. The Census Bureau recommends comparing releases whose years don't overlap.
- These are survey estimates, so they carry sampling error.

Source: ACS 2019 5-year (2015–2019) and ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), table B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, added up across all Texas block groups (state code 48).

The 2019 ACS 5-year release puts Texas's population at **28,260,856**.

Florida's estimated population went from **20,901,636** in the 2019 release to **21,216,924** in the 2020 release. That's an increase of **315,288 people (+1.5%)**.

| ACS 5-year release | Survey years | Florida population |
|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 2015–2019 | 20,901,636 |
| 2020 | 2016–2020 | 21,216,924 |
| **Difference** | | **+315,288 (+1.5%)** |

**This isn't a change from one year to the next.** Each figure is an average over five survey years, and the two releases share four of those years (2016–2019). The difference really just compares 2015 with 2020, spread across a five-year window. It shows the direction of growth but isn't the same as Florida's growth between 2019 and 2020. The Census Bureau recommends comparing 5-year releases that don't overlap, but this dataset only has these two. Both totals are also estimates, so they carry sampling error.

Source: ACS 2019 5-year (2015–2019) and ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over Florida block groups (GEOID prefix 12).

In Cook County, IL, the share of households with income under $25,000 went from **20.3%** in the 2019 release to **19.2%** in the 2020 release. That is about 1.1 percentage points lower.

| Release | Households | Under $25,000 | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2019 (2015–2019) | 1,972,108 | 401,095 | 20.3% |
| 2020 (2016–2020) | 1,991,474 | 382,543 | 19.2% |

**Why this isn't a clean one-year change:**
- **The survey years overlap.** The two 5-year releases share four of their five years (2016–2019). The difference really reflects swapping 2015 for 2020. The Census Bureau advises comparing periods that don't overlap.
- **The dollar basis differs.** Each release uses its own inflation-adjusted dollars: 2019 dollars versus 2020 dollars. So the $25,000 cutoff isn't exactly the same in real terms.
- **Sampling error.** These estimates have sampling error, so a gap this small should be treated with caution. I haven't tested whether it is statistically significant.

Source: ACS 5-year releases 2019 (2015–2019) and 2020 (2016–2020), table B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months). Under $25,000 = fields B19001e2 + e3 + e4 + e5, divided by the total B19001e1. Counts were summed over Cook County block groups (GEOID prefix 17031).

Source: ACS 2019 5-year (2015–2019) and ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over Ohio block groups (state FIPS 39) separately for each release.
